utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the logistical problems the Chamber was facing for a minute. After the first break, we'll come back to the issue dealt with in an e-mail, but at this moment the Defence is invited to proceed with the examination-in-chief of you, Mr. Krajisnik, but not until after I've reminded you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you find, please, if you've got -- you should have the same document that we finished with yesterday, marginal note 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I ought to note, Your Honour, that Mr. Krajisnik's got a file with him with a number of matters in it. It might be Your Honour might just want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just get the document out. Could you please just remind me of what document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it's the transcript of the second Serb Assembly Session, the one of the 21st of November, 1991. Yes, I understand Mr. Krajisnik, you're just extracting that for immediate purposes. And it will be towards the end. If you work from the back, Mr. Krajisnik, you should quite quickly come across a marginal note 17. So sorry, page 49 of the English. It's already up on the screen as well, from Mr. Slavojevic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found 16 but I really can't find 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If you go on about a page from 16, Mr. Krajisnik, you should find a heading that says that it was Mr. Velibor Ostojic who was speaking. If you find that name, it will be there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have empty pages here, so I guess that's the mistake. 114 and 115 is what I have, and 116, 117 -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether the booth can help, Your Honour. It's 49 of the English, but in the B/C/S it's a point where the assembly unanimously adopted the proposed decision on support to the JNA and mobilisation, and then Mr. Velibor Ostojic starts to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Should be page 52 of the B/C/S SA 01-205.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you catch that? Page 52, it should be, in your document. Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There is two parts. That was the problem. Unfortunately, it is not on page 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, fortunately you found it, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. On page 52 is 008681.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, have you found the bit where Mr. Ostojic starts speaking?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These pages are empty. Maybe that's causing confusion. See? This is 52. Yes. I received the page from the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good. Thanks to all concerned in sorting that out. Mr. Ostojic -- it says: "Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, members of the Assembly, dear guests, you just observed in several speeches by our deputies that we are mentioning the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The last speech was a blatant example of the way the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina treat the Serbian people in this republic. "Allow me several minutes to clarify my proposal with several examples. "Lately the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina, having inherited (the continuity of) the previous editorial policies, have been used for political power and pressure over the Serbian people and their representatives. "The Serbian people in BH are really under an information blockade. An enormous penetration of the media from other environments has resulted in recognisable undertones that are anti-Serbian and anti-Yugoslav in the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina. These undertones were reported uncritically from the media of war-engulfed Croatia; the media being anti-Serbian and anti-Yugoslav, have sown hatred towards the Serbian people and have sown such insults that really insult the Serbian people both as people and as a nation." Mr. Krajisnik, I don't know, you seem to be -- well, I don't know if struggling is the right word, but you seem to be having to find something still.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me it was the SDS Assembly and I put it in front of me. It must have been the Assembly of the Serbian people. Could you just tell me which document that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could help you out, Mr. Krajisnik, it is the assembly of the -- let me just see -- of the Serbian -- it's the Second Session of the -- the Second Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You'll find it at the bottom of page 52, going on to page 53, and the part that was read at -- with the words "nacionalno" on the third line of page 53. In the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will give you time to re-read it, the portion, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard Mr. Stewart and I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You'll wait for the question first probably, Mr. Krajisnik. So -- before you answer. Mr. Krajisnik, the question is: Had you -- you personally -- had you at this time noticed anything to support what Mr. Ostojic was saying that the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were really under an information blockade? And if so, what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shared the opinion of Mr. Ostojic, but I just wish to add one thing. Mr. Ostojic had worked in Radio and Television Sarajevo and had a lot more information, so that his contribution is better and more edifying than anything I could have learned from the media. Sarajevo newspapers and the media were imposing a blockade on Serb interests vis-a-vis what was going on in Croatia, so I do support the points made by Mr. Ostojic, but he had much better and broader information than I could have had as a regular citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what -- a blockade is a reasonably general word, Mr. Krajisnik. When you say that the media were imposing a blockade on Serb interests vis-a-vis what was going on in Croatia, are you able to be more specific about what the practical steps were that were being taken by the media?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prevailing impression among the Serbs is that the Muslim side got all the advantages and since their interests were closely linked with Croatia's interests, it seemed that all the information coming from Croatia that would have been to Serbs' advantage was blocked and only information favourable to Croats was allowed to seep through. A special problem was the radio and television in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbs had a lot of complaints about their reporting, as far as Serb interests are concerned. That problem, if I may add, still exists in the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the greatest number of the media that are located in Sarajevo, they are concentrated in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then further on, in this transcript, we see it's about a -- more than a page further on, it will be in both the English and the B/C/S. It's towards the foot of page 51 of the English. Do you see, Mr. Krajisnik, "Decision. The Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and the decision is decision on the motion to divide property of the joint television channels? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And over -- well, carrying on, it's over the page in the English, 52. That decision was apparently adopted. Was there -- was there anyone among the senior figures in the SDS who was primarily in charge of this particular issue about the media and such matters as this motion to divide the television channels?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that anybody was in charge, but I know that Mr. Ostojic was minister for information on the cabinet of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was his department on the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so he was probably the most concerned with the implementation of this decision that never actually came to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Had he actually been appointed by this time as minister, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic was minister for information on the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, media were under his competence. That was his province in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that was a slip in my mind, Mr. Krajisnik. He was subsequently appointed minister of information for Republika Srpska, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm talking about this time. He had been in a government of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the beginning, as minister for information. And then when the first government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina he got that post. But that happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, having only very recently asked you to find that document, you can now put that on one side because we are going to move on to a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are moving to the next session, the Third Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was dated the 11th, or held on the 11th of December, 1991. And, Your Honours, so far as we can track it, this transcript is not yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I see on the -- is it not P65 tab 62, the 11th of December? That's what my material says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We think those are just the minutes, Your Honour. Everybody stands to be corrected nearly all the time in relation to the paper in this case, but we believe those are the minutes rather than the more extensive item of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's the transcript, yes, yes. Thank you. Oh, yes. It's the stenographic record, yes. So therefore it needs a number, Mr. Registrar -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't resolve this issue with any precision. I can only add my recollection that this session was referred to at various times without -- by reference to what I understood as a pre-existing number. So at this point, I suppose we should add a number, but we will have to check to see if in fact it is a stenographic record rather than the minutes. The transcript received a number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript. Let me just check. The numbering -- there might be a difference, I don't know, but the numbering of this transcript seems to go from page 1 to 74, whereas the copy you provided us goes until page 75 but starts at page 2, whereas the other one started -- it looks very much the same but -- so therefore before we assign a number to it, let's just -- I'll use the two copies and see whether it's already in evidence, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we can certainly match the Prosecution for lack of precision at any point as we do here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, we'll proceed on this document. We've done the usual exercise of giving Mr. Krajisnik his own language version with marginal notes, just as a reference point. And Mr. Sladojevic has got copies available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, very early in this document, just to remind you, this is 11th of December, Third Session of the Assembly of Serbian people. Very early in this document, on about the first two pages, it's towards the bottom of page 4 in the English, there is a marginal note 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just inviting Your Honours please to note that as the lead in to where we are going. It's a recommendation to the armed forces on the preservation of the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. "1. The Assembly of the Serbian people gives its unreserved support to the Yugoslav People's Army and its efforts to preserve the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia within its border." And then I go to part of 2: "Proceeding from the role of the JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, under the constitution, the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina rightly expects the Yugoslav People's Army to extend all the necessary protection in the Defence of human lives and property in case of danger to Serb territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the Serb people as well as other peoples living in these territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina from whoever and from wherever it might come from and calls upon it to do so."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stewart repeat, please, this passage? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The whole passage. The French booth was not able to follow you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I really was trying to go sufficiently slowly but I'm requested. "Recommendation. To the armed forces on the preservation of the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. "1. The Assembly of the Serbian people gives its unreserved support to the Yugoslav People's Army and its efforts to preserve the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia within its borders and with the people wishing to remain in it..." And I didn't read then the last couple of lines. And going to 2: "Proceeding from the role of the JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, under the constitution, the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina rightly expects the Yugoslav People's Army to extend all the necessary protection in the defence of human lives and property in case of danger to Serb territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the Serb people as well as other peoples living in these territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina from whomever and from wherever it might come from and calls upon it to do so." And then, Mr. Krajisnik, you're the chairman there referred to, item 1 and so on. And then Mr. Slobodan Bijelic speaks. And the proposal he's putting before the meeting, we can pick up with the paragraph that begins -- it's capital letters in English, just below halfway down page 5: "Public appeal or request to the Yugoslav People's Army to defend with all the means at its disposal the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the citizens and material wealth in it as an integral part of the state of Yugoslavia in which a plebiscite was conducted of the Serbian people and other citizens at which they opted to remain in the joint state of Yugoslavia and a decision adopted -- and a decision adopted by the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territories of municipalities, local communities and settlements in Bosnia and Herzegovina which are considered to be the territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia." And then the next paragraph: "The appeal refers to the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina except for the territories of the municipalities of Grude, Ljubuski, Listica, Citluk, Kresevo, Posusje, Fojnica and Gornji Vakuf." But Mr. Krajisnik, what are the characteristics of -- well, indeed if they have such characteristics. What are the characteristics of those municipalities listed there which led them to be excepted from this particular appeal to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are municipalities with a Croat majority. And I suppose the plebiscite hasn't been organised there at all, nor did citizens express their will. That's the answer to your question. And if you need any more details, I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, without going to the maps, Your Honours will readily see from the maps we have that, for example, if I may just give this information, Grude, Ljubuski, Listica, they are down in the southwest of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so Your Honours would see from the maps where they lay in relation to Croatia. The -- then if you go to marginal note 3, Mr. Krajisnik, at -- it's page 6 of the English. Did you find marginal note 3, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it on page 6. 938 are the last digits -- 038.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. Krajisnik. Can you find a handwritten number 3 in the margin of your copy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's Mr. -- It's Dr. Milutin Najdanovic who is speaking. He says, if we -- well, he said: "It is dreadful even to think of the possibility that Germany might intervene in this war. Are we prepared for such a possibility?" Mr. Krajisnik, was that -- was that some -- was that some serious suggestion that Germany might actually become involved in action in a war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Certainly not. He meant the Second World War, making this comparison. The Yugoslav People's Army had a mission to defend Yugoslavia from outside enemies, outside aggressors, and he used Germany here in a rather clumsy way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It goes on: "If we manage to defend our territories, to give the majority of our people the chance to live together, have we studied all the alternatives this entails? Are we for a reduced Yugoslavia or are we for an integral Serbia? What would this community be with the Muslims and what without them? Will the so-called Serbian lands be a federation or will we be a unitary state of the Serbian people?" Was Mr. Najdanovic, was he including among those possibilities that he was mentioning, anything that could have been regarded as Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The answer is no. But Mr. Najdanovic was a university professor, married to a Jew, and as a professor of medicine he was trying to explain in a more philosophical way what that means. There is no connotation of Greater Serbia here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if you could say: What did you understand him to be meaning by the reference to an integral Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a period after the 14th of October, so the Assembly was already in place, Serb deputies had been outvoted, the rift had occurred, and various ideas are now on the table, and he says it's clear now we want Yugoslavia, Croats don't, Muslims don't. The only thing that remains is to see what's going to happen to those who want Yugoslavia. Is it going to stay one country, one land? How are we going to deal with the issue of minorities? So he's thinking aloud. The plebiscite had already happened. We expressed our will. We are telling the Yugoslav People's Army, please defend us now. What are we going to do with the other minorities? So he's sort of canvassing for ideas, looking for an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, that is probably reasonably clear to the Trial Chamber. My specific question, which I'm inviting you to concentrate, was his reference to an integral Serbia, one of a number of possibilities that he was mentioning in the way that you described. What did you understand him to be meaning by the mention of that particular possibility, among others, an integral Serbia? What did he mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were fighting against the unitarian Bosnia and Herzegovina. We wanted something decentralised. And now on account of this negative attitude we had towards a unitarianism and centralised authority, he's telling us we want the plebiscite -- you won the plebiscite, rather, now what kind of Yugoslavia do you want? Earlier, you offered the Muslim side something democratic, decentralised, et cetera. He didn't actually say it but that's what he was thinking. He was a very broad-minded man. He was recalling what we offered to the other side when we were thinking what to do with Bosnia. So he's kind of reminding us, "You had offered that earlier to the other side. You were against unitarianism then. So how can you be for a unitarian Serbia now?" So he was pointing out problems, making analogies with proposals we had made earlier on what kind of Yugoslavia we wanted. Simply something like before and after, what we wanted then and what we want now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you move on to find point 7? We are going to pass over a number of those marginal numbers. This is at the foot of page 12 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic is beginning a contribution here. I'm going to go about seven or eight paragraphs into what he says. Your Honours may note the first few paragraphs and the mathematical stuff in the contribution. Then a paragraph beginning: "When we think things over," which is just past the middle of page 13. "When we think things over, when we plan for the future, despite the fact that we will remain in Yugoslavia, I see that Bosnia cannot be organised like the other republics. Predominantly nation republics, because it is a republic with three national communities. And I ask that both in terms of language and terminology we adhere to this three national communities. "I had the opportunity when I was in Belgrade, before Vance came here, to spend an hour and a half alone with him. And then he called the three of us to a meeting. I should like to use this [community] today for the same purpose." Just pausing there, Mr. Krajisnik, can you say who "the three of us" were that Dr. Karadzic was referring to. That were called by Mr. Vance to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three sides are the Serbs, Croats and Muslims. And Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Kljujic are the three persons, I assume, because they are the representatives of the leading political parties, and they represent the three ethnic communities. I'm just guessing who it was, but these were the top people of the three national parties. I know that Mr. Karadzic was there, and I assume that the other two were at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then Dr. Karadzic continues: "To repeat constantly, three national communities, not three parties, but three national communities. "The parties represent these national communities, this time it is the Serbian Democratic Party, next time it might be the Federalists Party of Mr. Djokanovic. Some parties will act together. But the terminology should be: Three national communities because they exist. "In this Republic the life of the three national communities overlaps in places, in places they have things in common. But to my mind, the more separate things there are the better it will be. Perhaps these three national communities will very three school systems, perhaps even three health care systems, et cetera. Perhaps in formulating this recommendation we should state that in places where the Serbs are not able to preserve their civil, national, economic and other rights due to being vastly outnumbered, the Assembly of the Serbian people recommends that they form their municipality. In this way we would achieve what Mr. Milojevic vividly described for us, that we must not lose what we have taken, what we have invested in." Mr. Krajisnik, was it SDS policy at that time, 21st November, 1991, that the more separate things there were, the better?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two answers. One is that it was an answer to the moves made by the Muslim side. They outvoted us at their own initiative, violated the constitution, and now you don't want to be with us, we want to separate from you. Not literally but sort of. On the other hand, there was political marketing. Now that you've established your own assembly, now the leader of one party is disguising this in order to win this easier. Let's change this decision. Let's have the Yugoslav People's Army protect the Serbs where they are, without it being very obvious. Now, my understanding is that, in a way, this was a call to the other side, though there were some strings attached, see what we are going to do if we do not sit down and negotiate, in order to find a solution. Let me put it this way: We kept trying to get the others to talk things through because we realised that there can be no solution without an agreement of all three sides. There can be a short-term agreement but not a long-term agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I take it that you intended to refer to the date of the Third Session which is the 11th of December, not the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is completely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reference where Dr. Karadzic said in that passage I read: "Perhaps these three national communities will have three school systems." Now, in raising that possibility, Mr. Krajisnik, was it -- was it regarded by the SDS as a positive or a negative result if at the end of everything there were three school systems corresponding to the three national communities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'll try to explain this to you. We had one language, the Serbo-Croat language. When the new multi-party elections were held and when the new assembly was established, a problem cropped up straight away. The Croat side said, "we want to have a Croat language." The Bosniak side, "We have the Bosniak language." And now we ultimately had to say, "We have a Serbian language," although there are only nuances of differences. Even today there is a problem in Bosnia where there are different schools, where the curriculum is taught in the Croat language or in the Bosniak language. I still think it's one language. When I listen to the interpretation here, for instance, there are quite a few Croat words, purely Croat words that are used here, but it would be an ugly thing if I were to say, I can't understand the young man who is saying this, because I know the words. I lived there. So that is what he was saying, that from the very outset this is what was insisted upon, separating the languages. They even said that invitations to attend Assembly meetings should be sent once in Serbian, once in Croat, once in Bosniak, once in Cyrillic, in the Latin script and so on and so forth. So that is what he is saying, that ultimately we may have these separated systems because even if we didn't want it, others wanted it. This still exists. It's not big things that are big. Sometimes small things are big. And people create problems over these things unnecessarily. I mean, we who were there made these problems unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps I would be more direct about what I'm getting at here. Dr. Karadzic says, in two sentences, he says -- go to page 13 of the English: "But to my mind, the more separate things there are the better it will be. Perhaps these three national communities will have three school systems ..." Mr. Krajisnik, what I'm asking is whether, in saying that, Dr. Karadzic was referring to an SDS policy which had in mind that three school systems was something it ultimately wanted to achieve, as a positive thing, or whether it had in mind that it wished ultimately to avoid a situation where it was necessary to have three separate school systems? And I'm asking which of those was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't any of those two options. There was a third one. Mr. Karadzic was saying that once we talked to the other sides, perhaps we will indeed have the three school systems. The Croats wants to have their language, the Muslims want to have their language, the Serbs want to have their language. All three peoples feel that they haven't lived this through. They all want to have their own thing. So if we have that, then everybody will feel free to say now this is mine, because unfortunately, there was this conflict and then things were made artificially because of this conflict. Let me say one more thing. Our linguists -- I mean people who have a degree in the Serbo-Croat language and in literature, they kept saying all of this is the Serbian language. So there is no Croatian, no Bosniak, whatever. And then the others were irritated by that. So the answer is that Mr. Karadzic thought that if we are going to have many separate things, it will be better because everybody will say, look, this is my language, this is my thing, which is the way it is today. But on the other hand we don't need any interpreters. We understand each other. A lot of time has to go by, but it was to so topical at that point in time, let me just have my own language, or this other language, and so on. At one meeting of the Assembly, the distinguished Professor Filipovic said, "Are we going to use the Cyrillic or the Latin script, or the Cyrillic or whatever," so the Bosniaks were supposed to write in the Latin script. They said, and he said, "No, the Bosniaks want both the Cyrillic and the Latin alphabets because both are ours. You will see that at the first Assembly meeting." So the answer is that he is speaking about the consequences. And, of course, there were linguists who said, "Wait a minute, we want to have only our own language." But that is a discussion among experts. But we wanted least of all to have this separation along the lines of language, but the consequence was that we actually expected that. Because this wasn't necessary. The language existed before that too. And also the rules and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to invite you, because I'm not 100 per cent sure everything is all right with the English, so I'm going to invite you to read the next paragraph from your own language that begins "even the smallest municipality." It's only about four lines. I wonder if you would just read that out loud.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that. That's a recommendation for the Serbs where they feel threatened, where they feel jeopardised. They should establish --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I could make -- I'm inviting you to read that short paragraph out loud so we can have it interpreted today, the one that begins "even the smallest municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. It's written differently here. That's why I cannot find it, but yes, I have found it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 18 and then the line starting with -- "opstina."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. "Maybe in the formulation of this recommendation it should be said that where Serbs, due to ruthless outvoting, are not in a position to safeguard their civic, national, economic and other rights."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krajisnik, it's not -- that's not the paragraph I had in mind. It's the next one. I assume it's broken up into paragraphs in the same way. In English it begins "even the smallest municipality." It's about three, four lines. It's that paragraph. It's the next short paragraph that I'm inviting you to read out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "Even the smallest municipality can have three municipalities if we agree on that. If that is agreed on, at the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina that recommendations should state that this is not obligatory but it should be done unless national equality cannot be secured otherwise."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we've ended up with the same wording. It doesn't make any sense in English. I didn't want to comment. I just wanted to try and get it done. Well, I'll be direct about it, Your Honour. It makes no sense unless the word "unless" is changed to "if." Perhaps we could agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we hear from the interpreters that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is necessary to read the previous paragraph and that's why I tried to read it. I tried to read the previous paragraph, then you understand this better.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I probably understand the English better, Mr. Krajisnik. That's as much as we can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Krajisnik tries to explain, Mr. Stewart, that reading the two paragraphs together would make it more understandable. I'm not quite sure yet whether -- I leave it up to you whether you would like to invite Mr. Krajisnik to read the previous paragraph as well. I just try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. Josse makes a very sensible practical suggestion. Why don't we just send these two paragraphs, with respect, back to the CLSS and invite a new translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could do that and then -- but I have to then have to make one observation; that is, that we have two sources in B/C/S for this document. One of them being P64.A, tab 270, whereas the other source is P65, tab 62. The problem with these originals is that the numbering of the pages in the translations you provided to us, Mr. Stewart, differs from the one -- from some of them, at least these two versions, in some of them the first page starts with -- as the copy you provided us with, with the stenographic record of the Third Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in BiH, and then the second page being transcript of the Third Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereas some of the originals are provided with a translation where this first of -- could I say so -- the two cover pages is not translated, and that creates a difference in numbering in the English version by one page all through the document, whereas I see no other differences at this moment. We also see that -- yes. That's just -- So if you send it for translation, it should be clear what we send for translation. From what I see on my screen of the original of P65 -- no, P65, tab 62, we find it on the upper part of a page which is numbered page 18 and which bears the number SA 02 and then 4950. So that just for your information, that if it will be sent back that, that's the page on which this text appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would certainly follow Your Honour's direction, and that makes it -- just convinces me that we should send it to anybody in order to get it off our own desks, and we suggest that CLSS would be a good place. But thank you for that summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to read because it's an introduction, do you see point 8 in the margin -- sorry, I'll pause. Mr. Krajisnik, His Honour is engaged at the moment. I'm going to just have us wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you see marginal note 8 against which you are recorded as speaking, but the previous speaker was Mr. Nenad Veselinovic, and I think it makes sense of your contribution to look first at what he says. Toward the bottom of page 14 of the English: "I am in favour, and some perhaps remember that I insisted on Serb municipalities. But, we have not finished the process we started - that of regionalisation. "I think that the order of moves should be planned. Plainly speaking, to break up the existing municipalities where the Serbs are not a majority. For there are situations of some adjacent local communities, of settlements belonging to two municipalities where Serbs are not a majority. This means that from two or three neighbouring municipalities we have space to form a large, nice Serb municipality. "What I want to say is that the order of the moves should be decided, and that we should finish what we started - the separation of local communities, settlements, et cetera, and that an expert body should convene and state what can be done where. For instance in Sarajevo, we can form two Serb municipalities, or form another municipality between Sarajevo, Pale, Ilidza and Novo Sarajevo so as not to confuse our people. We will not finish what we have started. Now we will again put them in a position where we are forming municipalities and where some people do not understand that. Olovo has done it first, and it was done well, they passed a Decision to that effect and now they belong to the Serb Autonomous Region of Romanija, et cetera. "I suggest we finish the job we started. "I insist that the city of Sarajevo be first defined and that these municipalities be formed of the Serb settlements. I think that this sequence of events would speed up things, It would be more rational and practicable." And then you, Mr. Krajisnik, say: "Before anyone else takes the floor, let me remark that a misunderstanding is in question here. "In municipal assemblies where Serb representatives are in the minority, such as Novi Grad, Olovo, et cetera where decisions against the Serbian people are imposed on them by the majority, they should form municipal assemblies just like we formed the Assembly of the Serbian people here. This is what it is all about. "Everything else, regionalisation, is quite a different matter. "In a municipality like Olovo where we have a large territory and 20 per cent of the representatives we cannot allow them to be constantly outvoted and in that way decisions against the interests of the Serbian people to be imposed on them. All our further discussion will be the subject of the next item of the Agenda. "Only municipalities where Serbian delegates are a minority should form such assemblies as this Republican Assembly of ours is, so as to exercise certain rights. I think that this is the source of the misunderstanding. Veselinovic spoke about regionalisation, the rounding off of territories, like Mr. Vjestica and others are doing." So it was -- it was Mr. Veselinovic and Mr. Vjestica and some others who were misunderstanding the point, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They misunderstood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say what was the nub of their misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A municipality is one concept. That's a territorial concept, like a republic or like a state. But a municipal assembly is a body, like a parliament. We asked to establish assemblies in those municipalities where Serbs were outnumbered, a Serb assembly, that would discuss those matters where they had been outvoted. Now, this MP spoke about regionalisation, that now municipalities are supposed to be established. Basically that these entities should be set up. That was not the objective. The objective was to establish a body in those municipalities where Serbs were outvoted and outnumbered. That would be called a Serb assembly that could, just like this republican assembly, discuss various problems and adopt certain recommendations to the councilmen in terms of the areas where they were outvoted. It's a mistake that we didn't discuss the previous recommendation. The establishment of municipal assemblies, not municipalities. So that was the mistake. Now, Mr. Veselinovic meant regionalisation. That's what he thought, that certain territories should be established, but that was the wrong idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the -- you referred in your contribution there, you referred to: "... a municipality like Olovo, where we," that's obviously Serbs, "where we have a large territory and 20 per cent of the representatives [you] can't allow them to be constantly outvoted." But did the -- your position on this, did it only relate to municipalities where the Serbs had large territory, or did it relate generally to municipalities where the Serbs were in a minority and were being constantly outvoted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It related to all municipalities, where the Serbs were a minority and where they had been outvoted in an unconstitutional manner. It wasn't that they were outvoted on particular issues. As for the example of Olovo, I spoke about that either yesterday or the day before yesterday. You have a town there of 5.000 inhabitants and a municipality of 15.000 inhabitants. And now you have different villages. So in this small town, the majority is one ethnic group and the town is surrounded by villages with a majority population belonging to a different ethnic group. So the town can impose its own will on the entire municipality regarding things like water, roads, electricity and so on. So if a big municipality were to be transformed into several municipalities, then this meeting of a few villages would decide on certain things on their own. This was the example of Olovo of 20.000 inhabitants, but we have other examples too, but perhaps two-thirds of rural Olovo were Serbs. So the only problem was the municipal parliaments and what kind of decisions were being passed there, so that's why it was important to that could have this kind of assembly that could say, "Well wait a minute, this is not fair, this is not lawful, it should not be turned into a law." It was not an order to do this. It was a recommendation. It was for the councilmen themselves to decide in those places where they had been outvoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When -- if we go over, then, it's over the page in the English, to page 16, and it's to marginal note 9 on your copy, Mr. Krajisnik, where you're making a further contribution.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 8 and 10. Let me just see if I have 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to disappoint you. I don't have 9. I have 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I can recover immediately from my disappointment if you find the point in the text exactly halfway between 8 and 10, you contribute to the discussion: "Please, can we explain some things."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that page 22 in Serbian? Never mind. You go on. I see where I'm talking. Chairman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's it: "Please, can we explain some things." And then about four paragraphs down, you start: "In municipalities such as Novi Grad, Hadzici, Stari Grad." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I think if it would assist you, the page number 22 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The bottom, the second part of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are always of great help. Thank you. I found it. "We in municipalities like Novi Grad, Hadzici," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Mr. Krajisnik, yes. It says: "In municipalities such as Novi Grad, Hadzici, Stari Grad, et cetera, we have no rights whatsoever. It is there that assemblies of the Serbian people should be formed." Mr. Krajisnik, can you confirm, when you say "we have no rights whatsoever," in fact what you were saying, we do have rights, they are just being consistently overridden? That's what you were meaning to say, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I were to say, without any rights whatsoever, that would be wrong. You are right. Rights are being violated, and the way it's put here, there are no rights whatsoever, is an exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then Mr. Ostojic, who is the next speaker, in about the third paragraph of his contribution there, he refers to these same municipalities in a -- well, more or less the same municipalities. He says: "I think that municipalities such as Stari Grad, Hadzici, Srebrenica, Bratunac and many others." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "... and many others are actually something which is called the political self-punishment of the SDS." What did Mr. Ostojic mean by talking about "self-punishment of the SDS"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is said literally. He probably means the same thing that I meant, that it was outvoting, because SDS and SDA were sharing power in that area. I really don't know how to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krajisnik, if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self-punishment, it doesn't work, it doesn't seem logical to understand it as if SDS is punishing itself. Professors tend to like flourish. SDS cannot be punishing itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's move on and leave the professors behind for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik. And then point 10, I know you've got point 10, because you mentioned it a couple of minutes ago. "The chairman asked Mr. Ostojic," you see that? Middle of page 17 in the English. "The Chairman asked Mr. Ostojic what is the proposal and shall we opt for the establishment of Serb assemblies in municipalities?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then: "I think, said Mr. Ostojic, that my question also reflects my position. I believe that now we can take no other course of action. "In places where we can have no political influence ..." -- this appears to be Mr. Ostojic still speaking -- "where we can have no political influence on the life and work of the municipalities, in places where our representatives, Serb" -- "serve," I mean, "only" to fulfil the formal requirements for the functioning of a government which produces decisions against the interests of the Serbian people, municipal assemblies of Serb representatives must be formed. And in places where even this is not enough municipal territories of the Serb people must be constituted." It's that last bit I'm asking particularly about, Mr. Krajisnik, "and in places where even this is not enough municipal territories of the Serb people must be constituted," what specifically was Mr. Ostojic proposing in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was talking about a moment ago, the difference between municipality and municipal assembly. Mr. Ostojic was advocating the establishment of municipalities by dividing existing municipalities, and I am adding or rather saying, let us form new municipal assemblies rather than new municipalities. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this was on that point, from what you said, there was a -- at the very least there was a clear divergence of view, at least between you and Mr. Ostojic, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, eventually he agreed with me, although his original proposal had been different. But later he agreed that we should form municipal assemblies rather than new municipalities, because the latter was too radical. We were still hoping to find a moderate solution rather than going as far to form new municipalities. You are right in saying that originally his opinion differed from mine, but eventually he agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it -- was it at that time, 11th of December, can you say whether it was your view or Mr. Ostojic's view on this point which better reflected the view of the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be very sincere. This recommendation had a hard time passing through. The deputies were against any new municipal assemblies. They wanted regions. They thought that it was hopeless to hope for agreement with the Muslims. And we were giving one more chance to the Muslims and Croats, telling them, "We are just establishing a body to deal with national issues but let us sit down and see how to reorganise Bosnia-Herzegovina." So this recommendation to form municipal assemblies did pass through but with great difficulty. And further on in the discussion, there were many other speakers who said, on the contrary, "Let us form new regions instead."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go about one page on, to what you will have as marginal note 11, towards the top of page 18 of the English, we see a contribution from Mrs. Slobodanka Hrvacanin. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, of course, we have heard evidence from Mrs. Hrvacanin. She is from Zenica. I'm going to go straight to the fourth paragraph, although Your Honours, noting, because it's important as part of the lead-in for Your Honours' purposes, noting the previous paragraphs. But I go straight to: "Don't take it for granted that all Serbs are brave." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Don't take it for granted that all Serbs are brave, nor embellish things by saying that they are such in the central part of Bosnia because many of them were in favour of the plebiscite, but gave their vote through their friends so this would not be seen. What I want to say is that I would like to know how much we would win or lose by establishing such a Serb assembly. For, it is true that we are being outvoted." Mr. Krajisnik, we know that, because we've heard that Mrs. Hrvacanin was in a Serb minority municipality. She says then: "If we are to move, then all this discussion is pointless, but if we will remain living there, I would like to suggest that a commission draw up an appropriate model of action for central Bosnia, showing pros and cons." So Mr. Krajisnik, would it be fair to describe Mrs. Hrvacanin's position as lying somewhere between the view which you have just expressed as broadly the view of the SDS leadership, and the view of other deputies in this assembly who didn't like that proposal at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contribution of Mrs. Hrvacanin was very rational, very reasonable, and that was one of the reasons why we thought we should refrain from radical moves. Radical moves were proposed by deputies from areas where Serbs were in the majority, and they had no idea of what it was like to live when you were seriously outnumbered by other ethnic communities. And that's precisely what Mrs. Hrvacanin saying: You don't understand our situation and you want us to take a decision that would be against our interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could I ask Mr. Krajisnik to slowly read again the last part, the last sentence of this -- I think it starts with [B/C/S spoken]. Could you please slowly read that? You found that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read that one sentence only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "So if we were to establish such a Serb assembly, I would like to know how much we would win by doing that and how much we would lose, because it is true that we are being outvoted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we move on, then, Mr. Krajisnik, it's not very far. Again, it's about a page to where you find the marginal note 12? It's the middle of page 20 in the English. It's Mr. Momo Golijanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, do you think you could deal with that in some five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Golijanin says: "Mr. President, dear colleagues, all the discussions so far proceeded from a standpoint in which the Serbian people won. However, there are cases where the Serbian people is losing, so, what is to be done in such a situation? "For instance, in Nevesinje, there is an area called Gornje Polje, geographically the most beautiful part of Nevesinje where the Muslim people are in the majority, and they have expressed the wish to be annexed to Konjic. "Should they, for instance, be allowed to form their municipality, or should, for instance, Kula and Gacko, who have also expressed the wish to form their municipality with its seat in Mostar, be allowed to do so! What an anomaly? Gacko, Kula - with its seat in Mostar! "If we are demanding our rights in municipalities where we are in the minority it is only natural to expect that we give others rights in municipalities in which we constitute a majority. And, it is also questionable how the Serbian people will respond and react to such a position." Mr. Krajisnik, in Mr. Golijanin's reference to the Muslims having expressed the wish in that part of Nevesinje to be annexed to Konjic, does this reflect some similar debate going on within the Muslim political community in relation to the restructuring of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in a -- smaller measures than with Serbs. Both Croats and Muslims discussed it but less than Serbs. So it was said in jest, MAO, HAO and SAO. Like Muslim autonomous district, Croat autonomous district, Serb autonomous district. There are other examples when Muslims wanted to create their municipalities. Not municipal assemblies but municipalities. And even Croats in areas where they were a minority wanted their own municipalities. Of course, the war put a stop to all that. That such ideas had been voiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's finished that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until quarter past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, first of all I think I promised that I would come back to the issue of the -- dealt with in an e-mail of yesterday in open court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm also directly addressing you, Mr. Krajisnik. The Chamber has read the e-mail that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just this observation, of course, Mr. Krajisnik has no idea as to its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The issue you raised yesterday, you said, Mr. Krajisnik, in which you had a conversation with counsel has been addressed through an e-mail as announced yesterday, as you may remember, in court in which some further details were given. I take it these are the details provided by you, Mr. Krajisnik, to you, Mr. Josse. I think you sent the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I did, and Mr. Krajisnik provided the details to both of his counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Chamber has read the e-mail you have sent to us, Mr. Josse, in which the concerns of Mr. Krajisnik on the media reporting of his testimony were further explained. The Chamber will not intervene in any way. Any other position would require the Chamber to make an assessment of the reporting of the media on the correctness of their interpretation of your testimony. Mr. Krajisnik, where you have found some of the reports incorrect and unfair to you, any other position would also open the road for interventions, which would be unfair to the Prosecution. For this, but not only for this but for many other reasons as well, the Chamber decided to refrain from any intervention. The Chamber, speaking in very general terms and without an assessment on -- of any reporting on your testimony, Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber has not read, nor seen, any of these media reports, but the Chamber, speaking in general terms, has understanding for concerns any party may have about incorrect and unfair reporting. It is left to the parties to see whether and what action it deems appropriate to seek correction of what it considers to be incorrect and unfair reporting. The Chamber also appreciates that if the Defence would like to take whatever action, the input of Mr. Krajisnik might be relevant. Therefore, upon an application, whether or not in private session, the Chamber is inclined to positively respond to a request to allow communication of specific concerns Mr. Krajisnik may have to his counsel. I will draw the attention of the Registrar to the fact that you have raised these concerns, Mr. Krajisnik. This concludes an observation made by the Chamber on the matter. Then before I allow you to continue the examination-in-chief, Mr. Stewart, you may have noticed that I invited Mr. Krajisnik to re-read a certain line, a line being part of the observations made by Mrs. Hrvacanin, and that I did not really follow up to that line being read. I had some doubts on the translation. Of course, you quoted the translation, which is quite understandable, Mr. Stewart. It is the quote about "how much we would win or lose by establishing such a Serb assembly." Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wondered whether the translation, "Serb assembly," would be the right one. When I asked Mr. Krajisnik to read it again, then I got the same translation, but I found it important enough to verify during the break with some of the interpreters still available at that moment, which I could get hold of, to ask again whether the "establishing such a Serb assembly" should not be "establishing such a Serb municipality." And it was confirmed, but I'm seeking now confirmation from all booths that the word "opstina," which appears in that line as read by Mr. Krajisnik, that that should be translated as "Serb assembly" -- as "Serb municipality" rather than as both in writing and when it was repeatedly read by Mr. Krajisnik, "Serb assembly." So it should be "municipality," unless I'm now contradicted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is "municipality" in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, Mr. Stewart, you have put your questions on the basis of the written translation, I take it, which is not a correct one. It should be establishing such a Serb municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, I did put my question on the basis of the English translation which is all I can do, Your Honour. But, Your Honour, I'm grateful for that, clearly. If a translation error can be corrected, it's very helpful that it should. Your Honour, I probably had in mind myself, in not following that up, that page 15 of the English and Mr. Krajisnik's intervention, the paragraph was: "Only municipalities where Serbian delegates were in the minority should form such assemblies as this republican assembly of ours." So what was being talked about the terminology there, the same exercise that we are talking about was referred to as the setting up of Serb assemblies within a municipality. Therefore, Your Honour, it didn't -- what I'm saying is Your Honour, nothing struck me as amiss because whether the word "assembly" is used or the word "municipality" was used, the sense of it is -- can be perfectly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be perfectly correct, but a distinction has been made between establishing an assembly only or a municipality. The distinction appears, at least. Let's not further deal with it in detail. Let me first just verify, Mr. Krajisnik, you noticed that I asked to you re-read that portion. If -- when the question was put to you by Mr. Stewart on the intervention of Mrs. Hrvacanin, would your answer have been any different or perhaps did you -- did you give your answer on the understanding of the word "opstina" or did you -- when the question was put to you, did you understand it to be about the establishment of a Serb assembly? Could you ask -- could I ask you whether that needs any further explanation or would you say, well, that's how I had understood it, as the establishment of a Serb municipality and that was what I based my answer upon? If that's the case, we don't have to revisit the matter; if not, please add whatever you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I read exactly as it is written. What is written is "municipality." However, the translation was again "assembly." Mrs. Hrvacanin was reacting to the proposal of Mr. Ostojic, his original proposal to form municipalities. And I said I agree with Mrs. Hrvacanin. We cannot establish municipalities. We should form instead assemblies. That's what we need. The translation was wrong. She didn't want municipalities in Zenica. But I heard the interpretation; it was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just -- I especially since you made this distinction between "municipality" and "assembly" to be established, I thought it would be necessary to clarify this issue. It has now been clarified. We now well understood your testimony in this respect. And Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you find, please, point 13, numbered margin note 13 in your copy? Your Honour, this is page 20 of the English. It's a Mr. Milosevic. It's not Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. A Mr. Milosevic is speaking there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this Mr. Milosevic in the third paragraph, it is says: "In the municipality of Novi Grad there are 85 per cent more Muslims than Serbs. This means that Muslims outnumber the Serbs by 85 per cent. When outvoting is in question, the situation is as follows: We have 21 out of the total of 100 representatives. Outvoting in the Assembly and also in the government happens routinely. When we adopt decisions in the government we are outvoted in their interest. "It is in their interest for no organ to do any work, because their people are working for that. We are trying to prevent that - through whom? We have four Secretariats of which three are theirs: The Secretariat for Town Planning, for the Economy, and for National Defence. We only have the Land Survey Registry. "What is happening? "When the government sits in session, I interrupt the session. They remain and decide to take on ten new workers in the Secretariat for Town Planning, in which they already had more men. For instance, the head is a Croat, the head of the utilities department is a Muslim, the head of the inspectorate is a Muslim, they employ ten new people of whom eight are Muslims and two Serbs. They employ them at that session, an SDA session. "They say they had a majority and that that is the decision they adopted. That is how they make decisions. "In the territory of the municipality" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I invite you to restart reading from the line "for instance." I'm following the French translation, and you're really a couple of lines advanced to the French translation. You should really slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I will do that. "For instance, the head is a Croat, the head of the utilities department is a Muslim, the head of the inspectorate is a Muslim, they employ ten new people of whom eight are Muslims and two Serbs. They employ them at that session, an SDA session. "They say they had a majority and that that is the decision they adopted. That is how they make decisions. "In the territory of the municipality, we are trying to solve the issue of illegal construction. We Serbs there cannot do a thing. We demand that an inspection be carried out. They come, write a report, do nothing, and the building continues."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what is described there by Mr. Milosevic, was that typical of the sort of problems that were arising around Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. But this is about Sarajevo, where the problem was greater, and specifically in my municipality, where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you go, please, to point 15? It's about a page or so on. Actually, I'm going to go back, if I may, sorry, for one moment. Mr. Krajisnik, do you see number 14 in the margin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For us, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, towards the top of page 22 the paragraph beginning "I think that the proposal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you see a paragraph that begins "I think that the proposal"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that not number 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just close to number 14. Mr. Krajisnik, I wonder if could you read out loud that and the next two paragraphs? So three paragraphs in all, starting with "I think that the proposal."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I think that the proposal to form Serb municipalities is all right. I think that after that, we can go on talking about whether to annex ourselves to some entity or not or create a single region from two or three territories. "The chairman asks the deputies if it would be in order to propose the following: "Groups of deputies of the SDS municipal assemblies in BH, where decisions contrary to the interests of the Serb people are imposed by outvoting, are given the recommendation to adopt decisions on establishing municipal assemblies of the Serb people. "This should be additional and should be recommended only where necessary."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour will probably see I invited that passage to be read because it does draw that distinction between "municipalities" and "assemblies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's the distinction I see "skupstina opstine" which means, as far as I understand, "municipal assembly." There, "municipal" is used not as a -- how do you say that in English, not as a -- it's added to -- "skupstina," it's "assembly" but the assembly of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour is slightly losing me. Because Your Honour is introducing into the equation some superior knowledge acquired of the Serbian language, and so we are getting the interpretation from the booth, which made a -- which just came across in English with "municipalities" in one context, "assembly" in the other. Your Honour, perhaps we need to investigate this with our own B/C/S speakers and return to anything that needs clearing up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- I don't see that there would be, at least from what I read from the original, it doesn't give me the impression -- but again, as I earlier thought that I should verify with the interpreters, you're invited, Mr. Stewart, that if there is any doubt, since you have someone who speaks the language to verify that. Perhaps also either during the next break or now, if you need to have it done urgently, to look at it and then see whether there is any need for -- any need for our interpreters to review this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly wasn't thinking of there being an urgent need now or even as urgent as the next break, Your Honour. It's just something to be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will either hear from you or we'll just continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, just one thing, it was clearly -- it is clearly said here that they should establish a municipal assembly, a parliament, not a territory. The municipal assembly is a parliament. Not a municipality. Municipality is a unit like -- like a republic or something like that. So that is the difference. I hope I managed to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think as a matter of fact that we find two times in these lines, the last lines read, the words -- at least a combination of "skupstina" and "opstine," "skupstina" being first, and it's two times translated in English as a municipal assembly, and I do understand -- I would have no doubts on reading this -- and, first of all, I'm not a linguistic expert but it seems as if Mr. Krajisnik would fully agree. And let's proceed and see whether there is any further need to revisit the matter. If so, we'll hear from you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I agree completely, Your Honour. That's -- I'm perfectly happy to do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then can we take point 15 in the margin and start from there? This is Mr. Rajko. That's I take it that's his family name, Rajko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it's Rajko who?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kasagic says: "I therefore propose that serious work be done on the issue of regionalisation, not only as a political issue, but also as a strategic one, where we also have a specific goal. It is necessary to define not only the territorial relationships but also, economic, cultural and all other ones. And it is precisely in this respect that we have not done much. If we leave things as they stand now, the people in the field are left on their own. Everyone has their own vision. Everyone is trying to get to Belgrade, and do something there, establish links, et cetera, so we are losing the main links here. Simply, that is not the way that we can deal with the main problem." Mr. Krajisnik, what was Mr. Kasagic talking about when he said "everyone is trying to get to Belgrade, and do something there, establish links"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is being said is that there are different institutions of Yugoslavia in Belgrade. Now, every region, every individual goes to Belgrade to resolve certain problems for their own region. That's what he meant. I think that it is not right for each and every region to resolve its problems that way, but in a way, the interests of all regions should be represented, and that we should have a single body, which indeed happened ultimately, that would speak on behalf of all, because this way, all the regions were handling their own business as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then he continues: "At the assembly session held on 21st November, it was agreed to resolve the issue of the city of Sarajevo by a special decision. This is an extremely important issue. We still are not ready and we have to ask why. I personally do not know." That was correct, was it, Mr. Krajisnik, that no such special decision had been prepared?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please be a bit clearer? I don't know what this decision pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it appears that Mr. Kasagic is saying that at the previous assembly meeting, on the 21st of November, it had been agreed to resolve the issue of the city of Sarajevo by a special decision, but he appears -- say if this is wrong, Mr. Krajisnik, but he appears to be complaining that, in effect, this has not been progressed. Do you agree with that, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can move on. He says: "I am convinced that if we do not carry regionalisation through to the end and properly, it will have been better if we had done nothing at all. We will become a problem for ourselves. The people say: Either be a blacksmith and do your job properly or don't get your hands dirty at all. That is why I insist that this recommendation be incorporated in all this, that primarily, the problem be identified in municipalities with a minority Serb population and that this issue be solved in that context (also because of outvoting). "We have not done that. We are talking about the region of northern Bosnia (Doboj). Which region is that? We have enumerated 18 municipalities, of which only in two we have a majority. What regionalisation are we then talking about? "The other side will list the same, as will the third. And then we are at a stalemate. We should by all means bear in mind that they too have their scenarios and if they implement them without us reacting to everything that they want, I think that we can find ourselves at a disadvantage, for we already have several instances where the issue was raised of forming Muslim municipalities and we have no answer to that. Is it in our interest to form a municipality there? "Finally, I think that this should be linked with three items" -- I'm sorry: "Finally, I think that this should be linked with item 3 of the agenda, and within those conclusions we could postpone the adoption of this Recommendation, and decide on the conclusions and offered Recommendation after a discussion on item 3." And then you, Mr. Krajisnik, say: "The chairman states that it is evident that we either do not understand each other or fail to grasp the problems in municipalities where we are in the minority. In our discussions we all proceed from the situation in the area from which we come. "Gentlemen, there are urban areas where we cannot resolve this by regionalisation, because regionalisation is a completely separate issue." Mr. Krajisnik, is it fair to say that you were becoming exasperated by this point in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What particularly were the problems in municipalities where we are in the minority that you felt there was a failure to grasp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the proposal was, the objective was, to have a decision reached, a soft decision, a recommendation so that all those complaints that we received from the other municipalities would be given to these councilmen and that we have a Serb municipal parliament like in the republic, that we do not impose that. What is intertwined here are two ideas. As I said, we started regionalisation as a political move, in order to compel the other side to work with us in finding a real solution. I'm going to explain the meeting in Doboj. I'll probably be asked about it by the Prosecutor. All of these were political moves. Here, Mr. Kasagic is saying, "Seriously, let us link all of this up, and why don't we, at our own initiative, carry out a transformation of Bosnia?" I was against that. Here I asked for the recommendation to be made and to have these municipal parliaments where we had been outvoted and to offer the possibility of transforming Bosnia.
